Solution

Designing financial products that are trustworthy, compliant, and genuinely easy to use.

Financial products carry high stakes and high anxiety. Users need to trust the product before they'll act on it — and that trust is earned not through branding, but through clarity, consistency, and an interface that never makes them wonder if they made a mistake.

TU

TransUnion credit product design

BofA

Bank of America auto loans integration

Dense

Data-heavy dashboard and analytics expertise

15+

Years of high-stakes product design practice

The challenge

The challenge with financial products

The central UX problem in fintech is not complexity — it is anxiety. Users making financial decisions are operating in a heightened state of attention. They notice inconsistencies, they second-guess ambiguous labels, and they abandon flows that feel uncertain. Every piece of friction in a financial interface has a cost measured in drop-off rates and support volume.

At the enterprise level, fintech products face additional challenges: data density, regulatory requirements, multi-role workflows, and the need to surface complex analytical information in a way that supports decision-making rather than overwhelming it.

My approach

How I design for fintech

I design financial UX around progressive disclosure of complexity: start with the information the user needs to act, reveal depth when they ask for it. Dense data should be scannable — organized by decision priority, not by database schema.

Trust signals are explicit design decisions: confirmation patterns, transparent fee disclosure, error messages that say what went wrong and what to do about it. I treat every moment of user uncertainty as a design failure to be traced and fixed.

Key Patterns

How this shows up in the work.

Progressive complexity

Start with the summary. Reveal the detail on demand. Users who want to dig in should be able to; users who just need to act should not be made to.

Trust-building microcopy

Form labels, button copy, and error messages that are specific, honest, and actionable. Never 'Something went wrong.' Always 'What happened and what to do next.'

Data-dense dashboard design

Financial analytics dashboards that are scannable at a glance, drillable on demand, and organized around the questions users actually ask.

Compliance-integrated UX

Regulatory disclosures and consent flows designed as part of the experience — not as legal text bolted on at the end of a flow.

Error prevention in transactions

Confirmation patterns, summary screens, and explicit undo/cancel affordances for high-consequence actions. No user should feel uncertain about what they just did.

Multi-role financial workflows

Designing for the analyst, the approver, and the executive who all need different views of the same financial data.
